findings.title: Paradox's 'no victory condition' produces a score nobody reads and a campaign nobody finishes; the exceptions are the scores that gate a verb
findings.detail: EU4 (Paradox, 2013-) prints a running 'score' (monthly points from ADM/DIP/MIL ranks) and a Hall of Fame; players ignore both. What EU4 players did respond to were the two later systems that turned standing into access: Great Power rank (1.18 Rights of Man, Oct 2016: top-8 by total development, unlocking diplomatic verbs, and a grace period before you lose the seat) and Ages (1.20 Mandate of Heaven, Apr 2017: four fixed-window ages, each with seven public objectives, a Splendour currency, age abilities and a Golden Era). The community's 'no one finishes a campaign' complaint (a recurring r/paradoxplaza and r/hoi4 topic; HoI4 has literally no scoreboard and the 1948 end date is a dismissible popup) is a symptom of a score with no consumer, not of open-endedness per se. CK3 (2020) computes a legacy score at dynasty end and almost no one can tell you what is in it. Vic3 (1.0, Oct 2022) shipped 'objectives' (Economic Dominance, Hegemony, Egalitarian Society) as advisor-driven goal lists rather than scoring; they are a checklist the player forgets after the first hour, and forum consensus from launch was 'the game is over by 1900 because nothing counts after that'. Lesson for UGS: the checkpoint must feed something back into the sim (a slot, a legitimacy write, an event chain, a rank-gated verb) or it will be as inert as EU4 score.
findings.evidence: EU4 Rights of Man (1.18) dev diaries on Great Powers; Mandate of Heaven (1.20) dev diaries on Ages/Splendour; Vic3 1.0 objectives screen; CK3 game-over score screen; HoI4 end-date popup; r/paradoxplaza perennial 'do you ever finish a campaign' threads.

findings.title: Victoria 2's decomposed Great Power rank is the genre's best-legible scoreboard and its clearest snowball warning
findings.detail: Vic2 (Paradox, 2010) ranks every nation by prestige + industrial score + military score, shows the three terms side by side in the top bar and ledger, and makes rank consequential: top 8 are Great Powers with spheres and a grace period before demotion. Players understood exactly why they were rank 9 ('industrial score: build factories') and changed their build orders because of it, which is the behaviour UGS wants. The failures are equally instructive: prestige compounded (prestige-boosting techs and cheap war goals let the leader run away, 'prestige is king' was the community verdict), industrial score inflated late-game into meaningless six-digit numbers, and military score was farmable with battleship spam. Vic3 kept the rank ladder (Great/Major/Minor/Insignificant/Unrecognized) but derived prestige partly from being top producer of goods, which players immediately farmed with opium and tea. Rule: decompose into few named terms, show the decomposition, and cap or reset each term per era so the leader cannot compound it.
findings.evidence: Victoria 2 ledger 'Rank' tab (prestige/industry/military columns) and Great Power grace-period rule; Vic3 prestige-from-goods (1.0) and the 'opium prestige' complaints on the Paradox forum and r/victoria3 late 2022.

findings.title: Twilight Struggle is the only shipped Cold War scoring design that demonstrably changed every decision, and it did it with a bounded track, known scoring moments, attribution of catastrophe, and a handicap instead of a second rulebook
findings.detail: Twilight Struggle (GMT, 2005, Gupta & Matthews): one VP track from -20 to +20; +20 is an automatic win at any moment; final scoring after turn 10 scores every region with the same Presence/Domination/Control table UGS already uses (battlegrounds decide ties); Europe Control at scoring is an instant win; holding a scoring card at end of turn loses the game; failing the per-turn Military Ops requirement (set by DEFCON) costs VP; and DEFCON 1 ends the game with the player who caused it losing, regardless of the track. Asymmetry (USSR early, USA late; different card decks) is handled with a single board and scoring table plus an influence-bid handicap, never a second scoring system. Player behaviour: every operation is priced in 'what does this do at the next scoring', the DEFCON rule creates a real 'don't be the one who triggers it' discipline, and the auto-win threshold creates urgency in a game that would otherwise run out the clock. Known failure modes to design around: 'DEFCON suicide' plays (forcing the opponent to fire an event that drops DEFCON on their turn, e.g. via headline ordering, and Wargames as an intentional end-the-game card), scoring-card timing races, and the fact that TS is strictly two-player: minors are terrain, not players.
findings.evidence: Twilight Struggle rulebook (Deluxe Edition, GMT 2009): sections on Victory (auto-win at 20 VP, DEFCON 1 loss attribution, Final Scoring, held-scoring-card penalty), Military Operations requirement, regional scoring tables; BGG strategy forum threads on 'DEFCON suicide' and bidding influence as handicap.

findings.title: Era-scored 4X (Civ VI Rise and Fall, Humankind, Civ VII) proves per-era reset kills the snowball and that a threshold scaled to expectation is what makes the score fair across unequal players; it also shows the checklist and sprint failure modes
findings.detail: Civ VI Rise and Fall (Firaxis, Feb 2018, Ed Beach explicitly targeting Firaxis' own telemetry that most games are abandoned mid-way) resets Era Score every era; the Golden/Dark threshold is set per era and scaled by the civ's own recent performance, so a laggard is graded against its own pace, not the leader's; a Dark Age is not a loss but a different toolkit, and Heroic Age rewards recovering from one. Players changed behaviour: they timed wonders, city founding and great-person recruitment to era boundaries. Failure: hoarding Historic Moments across the boundary (the 'sprint' problem), and Dark-Age-on-purpose farming. Humankind (Amplitude, 2021) made cumulative Fame the single score with era stars; because Fame never resets, the ancient-era leader stays ahead and players sat in early eras 'star farming'. Civ VII (Feb 2025) went furthest: three Ages with hard transitions, four public Legacy Paths per age with milestone thresholds, and resets at the boundary; reception was split exactly along the axis UGS must watch: praise for 'I always know what counts' and anger at 'checklist feel' and 'my progress got reset'. Extract: reset per era, grade against expectation, publish the criteria, but express the criteria as standings and verdicts, never as a to-do list.
findings.evidence: Civ VI Rise and Fall Era Score/Ages rules and Ed Beach's 2017-18 interviews on unfinished games; Humankind Fame/era-star system and the 'ancient era camping' meta on the Amplitude forums; Civ VII Legacy Paths and Age transitions, Steam/press reception Feb 2025.

findings.title: Cold War-specific precedents (Balance of Power, Crisis in the Kremlin, Hidden Agenda, Supreme Ruler Cold War, Superpower 2) put prestige on crises and deliver the verdict as prose from biased sources
findings.detail: Balance of Power (Chris Crawford, Mindscape 1985; 1990 Edition) is the direct ancestor: a two-superpower game over an eight-year term where the only score is prestige, written almost entirely by crises (backing down costs prestige in proportion to how far the confrontation escalated; the winner is the higher prestige at term end; nuclear war ends the game with the 'we do not reward failure' screen and no score). The 1990 Edition added a Nastiness Index so provocation itself was tracked, which is the answer to TS-style 'make them pull the trigger' play. Crisis in the Kremlin (Spectrum HoloByte 1991) and Hidden Agenda (Springboard 1988) scored a single-nation leader with faction approval ratings and an ending delivered as press verdicts from several sources with different biases (Hidden Agenda's 'history's judgment' bulletins), which is exactly the epistemic newspaper UGS already has. Supreme Ruler Cold War (BattleGoat 2011) scored a sphere-of-influence tally but only for the USA/USSR campaign, so minors had no stake; Superpower 2 (GolemLabs 2004) let the player pick an objective set (economic/military/political) evaluated on a date and ended the game by domestic overthrow when approval collapsed, which was gamed immediately because approval was cheap to buy. Extract: prestige is a crisis ledger, not a passive accrual; the campaign verdict is prose from named voices; and a nation's own fail state is domestic, which is how minors get a stake without a second scoring system.
findings.evidence: Balance of Power manual (1985) and Crawford's Chris Crawford on Game Design (2003) chapter on BoP; Balance of Power 1990 Edition Nastiness Index; Hidden Agenda (1988) end-game press verdicts; Crisis in the Kremlin (1991) faction ratings; Supreme Ruler Cold War (2011) sphere-of-influence victory; Superpower 2 (2004) objectives and overthrow condition.

findings.title: Narrative-verdict games (Suzerain, Terra Invicta objectives) show that a categorical verdict with named consequences is read and replayed for, while a distant numeric win condition is not
findings.detail: Suzerain (Torpor Games, Dec 2020) ends with an epilogue that grades the term by topic (economy, constitution, welfare, foreign policy, the fate of named characters) as prose slides computed from hidden flags; there is no number and no ranking, and it is one of the most-discussed endings in the genre precisely because every sentence names a decision the player made. Terra Invicta (Pavonis, EA Sept 2022) gives seven asymmetric factions their own win condition plus a shared objective ladder with resource rewards; the objectives are praised as the tutorial spine but the win conditions are 100+ hours away and most campaigns are abandoned after the mid-game plateau (the 'I stop at turn 200' problem in another skin, same as Stellaris' default victory year 2500 that most players never reach and whose composite score screen the AI does not even pursue). Extract for UGS: the unit of scoring output is a verdict sentence per term that names the cause ('EUROPE HELD: NATO ACCESSION OF WEST GERMANY, 1955'), and the checkpoint cadence (every five game-years) is the answer to the abandonment curve because each reckoning is a satisfying stopping point that is also a resumption point.
findings.evidence: Suzerain epilogue system (2020); Terra Invicta faction victory conditions and objectives ladder (2022 EA); Stellaris victory-year setting and Victory Status screen, r/Stellaris 'never reached the victory year' threads.

findings.title: The failure state must be un-winnable by construction: DEFCON's kill-ratio scoring is the counterexample, Twilight Struggle's attribution and Crawford's refusal are the model
findings.detail: DEFCON (Introversion, 2006) scores a general exchange (default mode 2 points per million enemy dead, -1 per million own dead, plus Genocide and Survivor modes), which makes the exchange a game to win and teaches first-strike optimisation; it is a great ten-minute game and precisely what UGS says it is not. Twilight Struggle assigns the DEFCON 1 loss to whoever caused it, Balance of Power refuses to show any score at all, and the existing UGS nuclear research (principle 10) already commits to 'score is how long you kept it'. The one addition the genre suggests is limited use short of exchange: Balance of Power's Nastiness Index and TS's Military Ops floor show that provocation and taboo-breaking should be a permanent ledger entry on the era grade, so that a battlefield weapon that 'wins' Korea still caps that era at a pyrrhic grade for the user and lowers legitimacy for the rest of the campaign.
findings.evidence: DEFCON (2006) scoring modes; Twilight Struggle DEFCON 1 rule; Balance of Power nuclear-war ending; docs/research/nuclear-weapons.md principle 10 in this repo.

findings.title: Rules a checkpoint-scored Cold War campaign must obey (extracted)
findings.detail: 1. Every score term owns a verb the player can pull this month, and the checkpoint writes something back into the sim (EU4 Ages/Great Powers, Vic2 rank; not EU4 score, CK3 score, Vic3 objectives). 2. Few named terms, decomposition always visible, expressed as bands and words (Vic2 three columns; never Humankind's six-digit Fame). 3. Reset per era and grade against expectation, not against the leader (Civ VI era score and scaled thresholds; not Humankind cumulative Fame or Vic2 compounding prestige). 4. One board, one table, asymmetry by baseline/handicap (Twilight Struggle bid, Civ VI per-civ threshold), never a second scoring system per faction (Labyrinth, Wir sind das Volk and Terra Invicta needed bespoke asymmetric win conditions and got a harder-to-learn game). 5. Scoring moments are public, dated and unavoidable, and measure a held state, not a snapshot, so the sprint before the date is worthless (TS final scoring known from turn 1; Civ VI moment-hoarding is the failure). 6. Catastrophe is attributed and un-winnable: the trigger-puller loses, everyone else's record freezes, provocation is a ledger (TS, Balance of Power, Nastiness Index; reject DEFCON). 7. The verdict is prose from a named voice with a cause (Suzerain, Hidden Agenda, Vic2 ledger), and a foreign standing is an estimate until the record is frozen (UGS house rule, no precedent got this right). 8. The AI rival must play the same scoreboard (Stellaris AI ignores victory score, so score is meaningless; UGS's influence allocator already does this for one term and must for all of them).
findings.evidence: Synthesis of the games above; Labyrinth: The War on Terror (GMT 2010) and Wir sind das Volk! (Histogame 2014) as the asymmetric-win-condition counterexamples.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: THE RECKONING: one scoreboard of four era terms, graded per era against the deterministic hands-off baseline
mechanics_recommendations.why: Solves (d) without a second system: the same four terms apply to every nation, and asymmetry is handled by grading each nation against what the untouched sim produces for it at that checkpoint (the sim is deterministic, so the baseline is a fixed table generated at ship time, like Civ VI's per-civ era threshold or the TS influence bid). The USSR is judged against Stalin's USSR, Egypt against Nasser's Egypt, and a Western minor shares its bloc's alignment term rather than needing its own. Per-era reset kills the Vic2/Humankind snowball.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Terms, each reading state that already exists: ALIGNMENT = the standing of your column (West/East/Denied) in the frozen Checkpoint (a non-aligned player scores on the DENIED column, so denial is a real strategy); SYSTEMS = own industrial output and living-standard band relative to the rival pole's (planners see REPORTED figures, the reckoning prints the true one as 'the record'); STANDING = legitimacy band plus the crisis ledger (backdowns and provocations, Balance of Power style; no new currency); THE PEACE = catastrophe terms: years without general exchange, taboo intact, wars settled vs frozen. Each term is graded in one of five words (TRIUMPH / ASCENDANT / HOLDING / ECLIPSED / HUMILIATED) by comparing the held value to the baseline table with a tolerance band; the era grade is the median of the four terms with THE PEACE able to cap it (any first use caps the user at ECLIPSED). Store per-era grades in a `Reckonings` resource; store the baseline as generated scenario data, never hand-edited. Cheap: four comparisons per checkpoint per nation.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Held-state scoring: the checkpoint reads the trailing 12-month standings ring, not the January snapshot
mechanics_recommendations.why: Known scoring dates create a sprint (Civ VI moment-hoarding, TS scoring-card timing, the coup launched in October 1954 to flip a battleground before the freeze). Measuring what was held over the preceding year makes last-minute plays worth one-twelfth and rewards the patient program, which is the historically true shape and the one the influence design's hysteresis already wants.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Standings are already recomputed monthly; keep a 12-entry ring per region and per bloc-total, and freeze the ring's majority verdict at the checkpoint. The paper prints 'HELD FOR n OF 12 MONTHS' next to each regional line so the player sees why a December coup did not count. Same ring for the SYSTEMS term (12 monthly output samples). Determinism: a Vec in the Influence resource, digest-folded like the checkpoints.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: The checkpoint writes back into the sim: grades change slots, legitimacy and domestic events
mechanics_recommendations.why: The genre's inert scores (EU4 score, CK3, Vic3 objectives) failed because nothing consumed them; the ones that changed decisions (EU4 Great Power verbs, Ages/Splendour, Vic2 rank) gated capability. UGS's house rule 'no panel without a verb' applies to the score too: the reckoning must be a cause, not only a record. It also gives minors a domestic stake without a second scoring system (Superpower 2 overthrow, Crisis in the Kremlin removal, the 1964 Khrushchev ouster and Suez 1956 as history).
mechanics_recommendations.how: ASCENDANT or better on the ALIGNMENT term grants one influence slot (the EU4 Splendour analogue, bounded, no currency); ECLIPSED or worse on any two terms fires a domestic pressure event chain (Politburo/Cabinet/Junta variant chosen by the existing regime type: a leadership challenge with priced options, never a game over); HUMILIATED on STANDING debits legitimacy for the next era. The AI superpower reads its own grade and reallocates (raises AID tier where it is ECLIPSED), which is what makes the standings adversarial and the score meaningful (the Stellaris-AI-ignores-victory lesson). All writes go through existing effect grammar (GrantInfluenceSlot, event triggers, legitimacy).

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: The campaign verdict at 1970 (and at catastrophe) is a dated prose verdict from named voices, printed as the final edition of the paper
mechanics_recommendations.why: Suzerain, Hidden Agenda and Balance of Power show that a verdict people quote is prose with causes, and UGS already owns the epistemic newspaper. A final number would be ignored; a final edition with three bylines (your own organ, the rival's organ, the non-aligned Gazette) turns the four era grades and the hinge events into a story, and the general-exchange funeral already exists for the failure branch.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Final edition sections: THE RECORD (the four reckonings as a 4x4 grid of grade words with the baseline comparison as 'AHEAD OF / AS / BEHIND HISTORY'); THE HINGES (the three wire lines with the largest weighted delta on each term, pulled from the existing wire ring and command log, with dates); VERDICT (one sentence per byline, templated from the grade sequence: e.g. 'THE OBSERVER: THE PEACE HELD AND THE SOCIALIST CAMP GREW; THE HERALD: A DECADE OF RETREAT IN ASIA; THE GAZETTE: THE NEW NATIONS STAYED THEIR OWN'). On general exchange the final edition is replaced by the funeral and every nation's verdict is 'THE PEACE FAILED, YEAR n', with the attribution chain and no grades: the only score is years kept, exactly as nuclear research principle 10 commits. Foreign grades print through political penetration as estimates until the frozen record, then as the record.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: A permanent provocation ledger on THE PEACE term so 'make them pull the trigger' does not pay
mechanics_recommendations.why: Twilight Struggle's DEFCON attribution alone invited DEFCON-suicide plays that force the opponent to trigger; Balance of Power's 1990 Nastiness Index is the fix: provocation is tracked whoever fires. UGS needs this or the optimal play against the AI becomes 'drive tension to Brink and let it be the initiator'.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Each tension write already has a named cause and an author; accumulate per nation the tension it authored above the Crisis band into a provocation count, printed in THE WORLD IN NUMBERS as a band (RESTRAINED / FORWARD / RECKLESS). At each checkpoint RECKLESS caps THE PEACE at ECLIPSED even if no war happened; at general exchange the funeral names both the initiator and the highest provoker. No new currency: it is a counter over existing tension events.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: A monthly STANDINGS box and a PACE line in the paper, with the next reckoning date on the HUD
mechanics_recommendations.why: Score must be visible where the player already looks and in words, with no per-tick jitter (house rules); Civ VI's always-visible era-score bar and TS's VP track are the two scoreboards players actually watched. Between checkpoints the player needs a leading indicator, not the frozen record.
mechanics_recommendations.how: THE WORLD IN NUMBERS gains three lines: STANDING (this month's provisional grade words for the four terms, own figures exact, rival's as estimates with the coverage bracket), PACE (quarterly, one word per term versus the trailing ring: GAINING / STEADY / SLIPPING with the top cause word), and NEXT RECKONING: 1 JAN 1955 (n MONTHS). The politics panel's battleground list gets a filter chip COUNTS AT RECKONING. Clicking STANDING opens the dossier page for the score with the four terms as a signed ledger of causes, the same shape as the country dossier.

pitfalls: Score watching and farming: any term that accrues from a cheap repeatable act gets farmed (Vic2 prestige from cheap war goals, Vic3 goods prestige, Humankind era stars). Every UGS term must read a held state (standings, output band, legitimacy) not an event count, and the provocation ledger must be the only counter.

The snowball: cumulative scores (Humankind Fame, Vic2 prestige compounding via tech) crown the 1955 leader for the whole campaign. Grade per era against baseline, reset, and let the rival AI reallocate against its worst term.

The checklist feel and reset resentment (Civ VII Legacy Paths, Vic3 objectives): if the reckoning reads as a to-do list the game becomes homework, and if a reset erases visible progress players feel robbed. Express criteria as standings and verdicts, keep the standings map painted continuously, and reset only the grade, never the map.

The historical baseline as a script leak: grading against the hands-off run must never print what history did ('Cuba went East in 1961'); print only AHEAD OF / AS / BEHIND HISTORY per term, and keep the baseline table in generated data with no per-country rows shown to the player.

DEFCON suicide and AI-as-initiator: without a provocation ledger the optimal play is to make the AI fire first so the attribution falls on it; conversely a too-cheap reckless cap punishes a defender who was forced to Brink. Author attribution must follow who wrote the tension, not who was at the table.
Inert score: if nothing in the sim consumes the reckoning it becomes EU4 score. Ship the write-backs (slot, domestic chain, legitimacy) with the first version, or ship nothing.

Numbers where words belong: the temptation to print '73.4 points' or a percentile rank. Five grade words, three pace words, three standing verdicts; the exact figures live only in the dossier ledger as signed causes.

A superpower-only scoreboard (Supreme Ruler Cold War, Twilight Struggle): minors must see their own column and their own SYSTEMS and STANDING terms in the first hour or they will conclude the game is not for them; the 'NO STANDING PROGRAMS: MINOR POWER' reason must be paired with a term they can move (denial, living standard, legitimacy).
analysts.first_hour_test: Founding edition (1 Jan 1950): the paper carries a box THE RECKONING OF 1955 stating in four lines what will be counted (ALIGNMENT of your column, SYSTEMS, STANDING, THE PEACE), each with the nation's opening position in words and its verb ('ASIA: PRESENCE, CONTESTED. VERB: AID, PRESENCE. NEXT: KOREA, ELECTIONS MAY 1950'), and NEXT RECKONING: 1 JAN 1955 (60 MONTHS) on the HUD. By the June 1950 edition the player must have seen: a monthly STANDING line with provisional grade words and the rival's as an estimate with a coverage bracket; at least one PACE line (the April quarterly) with a cause word they recognise from their own action or from a wire line ('SLIPPING: SOV AID, INDIA'); one decision explicitly priced in a term (the Korea intervention card should say which term it protects and which it spends: ASIA standing versus legitimacy and THE PEACE); and, if playing a minor, their own column named (DENIED for a non-aligned player) and one of SYSTEMS or STANDING they can move now. At the first checkpoint (Jan 1955) the paper prints THE 1955 RECKONING as a full page: the four terms as grade words with AHEAD OF / AS / BEHIND HISTORY, the regional standings with HELD n OF 12 MONTHS, the rival's grade as the frozen record (no longer an estimate), the three hinge wire lines with dates, one verdict sentence per byline, and what the reckoning changed ('ONE INFLUENCE SLOT GRANTED' or 'THE POLITBURO IS UNEASY'). The player should be able to say in one sentence how they are doing and what they will do differently in the next era; if they cannot, the score has failed the house rules.

findings.title: Contemporaries tracked six dimensions, and the two blocs headlined different ones with the same underlying facts
findings.detail: Across 1947-1970 the documents both governments actually wrote to answer 'are we winning' converge on six things: (1) the STRATEGIC BALANCE, always as an estimate of the rival (the 1955 'bomber gap' after the Tushino flyby, the 1957-61 'missile gap'); (2) ECONOMIC MOMENTUM, tracked as growth RATE by the Soviets and as absolute level plus consumer standard by the Americans (GNP race, Kitchen Debate); (3) the THIRD WORLD COUNT / alignment ledger, including UN General Assembly roll-calls and the domestic 'who lost X' politics of a country leaving your column; (4) PRESTIGE, measured from 1954 by USIA foreign opinion surveys and then by science/space firsts, Olympic points tables, exhibitions and competitions; (5) BLOC COHESION, meaning discipline inside your own camp (Suez 1956, Hungary 1956, the Sino-Soviet split, de Gaulle's 1966 NATO exit, Czechoslovakia 1968, the Berlin refugee 'vote with their feet'); (6) CREDIBILITY, the outcome of crises framed as who blinked (Berlin 1948/1958/1961, Taiwan Straits 1954-55 and 1958, Cuba 1962) and later Vietnam's 70%-for-reputation logic. The Soviet composite for all six was the 'correlation of forces' (sootnoshenie sil): a deliberately non-military aggregate counting the socialist camp, the national-liberation movement and the working class of the capitalist states as weights. The American composite was NSC-68's zero-sum 'a defeat of free institutions anywhere is a defeat everywhere'. Same world, two headline metrics: the planner headlines rate and the Third World count; the market headlines level, allies and votes. This is the historical warrant for one scoring system with a bloc-flavoured newspaper front page.
findings.evidence: NSC-68 (14 Apr 1950, FRUS 1950 vol. I) sections IV and IX compare US and Soviet GNP, military share of GNP and stockpiles side by side; Gaither Report 'Deterrence and Survival in the Nuclear Age' (7 Nov 1957); USIA Office of Research reports 1954-1960 (NARA RG 306) and Kenneth Osgood, 'Total Cold War' (2006) ch. 3; Khrushchev's report to the 20th Congress (14 Feb 1956) and the 1961 Party Programme on the correlation of forces; Zubok & Pleshakov, 'Inside the Kremlin's Cold War' (1996); Fursenko & Naftali, 'Khrushchev's Cold War' (2006); McNaughton memo to McNamara, 24 Mar 1965 (Pentagon Papers, Gravel ed. vol. III).

findings.title: Calibration list: 24 dated score events, who claimed the point, and how far elite and public perception moved
findings.detail: Magnitudes: SEISMIC / MAJOR / MODERATE / MINOR, elite vs public. 1) 23 Sep 1949 Truman announces the Soviet A-bomb (RDS-1, tested 29 Aug 1949) — Soviet point; US elite SEISMIC (H-bomb decision 31 Jan 1950, NSC-68), public MODERATE. 2) 1 Oct 1949 PRC proclaimed, after the China White Paper (5 Aug 1949) — Soviet/Chinese point ('one third of humanity'); US public MAJOR via 'who lost China' (McCarthy's Wheeling speech, 9 Feb 1950); the first loss-attribution scandal of the era. 3) 25 Jun 1950-27 Jul 1953 Korea — Inchon (15 Sep 1950) a US claim; Chinese intervention (late Nov 1950) the 'worst US defeat'; armistice a draw scored as a loss at home (Truman's Gallup approval 22% in Feb 1952; Eisenhower's 'I shall go to Korea', 24 Oct 1952) and as a SEISMIC prestige win for Beijing in Asia. 4) 19 Aug 1953 Iran and 27 Jun 1954 Guatemala — covert US wins: elite MODERATE confidence, public ZERO; deniable wins score privately only. 5) 12 Aug 1953 Soviet thermonuclear test — Moscow claims parity; US elite MODERATE until Castle Bravo (1 Mar 1954). 6) 7 May 1954 Dien Bien Phu, Geneva Accords 21 Jul 1954 — Western loss MAJOR for France, MODERATE for the US ('loss of North Vietnam'); SEATO (8 Sep 1954) booked as compensation. 7) 18-24 Apr 1955 Bandung — the non-aligned field appears; Zhou Enlai's point; Dulles's 'immoral neutrality' (9 Jun 1956) shows Western elite MODERATE alarm. 8) 27 Sep 1955 Czech-Egyptian arms deal and the Nov-Dec 1955 Khrushchev-Bulganin tour of India, Burma, Afghanistan; Bhilai steel (Feb 1955), Aswan financing (Oct 1958) — the 'Soviet economic offensive'; CIA counted aid commitments as a score line (Allen Dulles speech, Jan 1958); Western elite MAJOR. 9) Oct-Nov 1956 Suez and Hungary in the same fortnight — Suez a Western prestige loss MAJOR (Britain/France forced out; Eisenhower Doctrine 5 Jan 1957 to plug the hole); Hungary a Soviet legitimacy loss MAJOR in Europe (PCI and PCF defections, Sartre's 'Le fantome de Staline') but MINOR in the Third World (Nehru barely protested). Both sides lost a point in the same month: zero-sum failed. 10) 4 Oct 1957 Sputnik (Sputnik 2 on 3 Nov; Vanguard TV-3 explodes 6 Dec) — SEISMIC, the largest single prestige swing of the era; USIA's 'Impact of Sputnik' surveys (Oct-Nov 1957) found Western Europeans now rated Soviet science ahead; Eisenhower's approval fell roughly twenty points over the following months (Gallup); NASA (29 Jul 1958) and NDEA (2 Sep 1958) were the policy response. 11) 7 Nov 1957 Gaither Report, leaked to the Washington Post 20 Dec 1957 ('Secret Report Sees U.S. in Grave Peril') — the 'missile gap' narrative: Kennedy's Senate speech 14 Aug 1958, Alsop's columns projecting 3:1; elite belief MAJOR and false, corrected privately by U-2 (from Jul 1956) and Corona (from Aug 1960), publicly by Gilpatric's Hot Springs speech 21 Oct 1961. 12) 31 Jan 1958 Explorer 1; Apr 1958 Van Cliburn wins the Tchaikovsky Competition in Moscow; Brussels Expo (Apr-Oct 1958) pavilion duel — US recovery MINOR-MODERATE; soft prestige events counted. 13) 14 Jul 1958 Iraqi revolution — Baghdad Pact loses its capital; Western loss MODERATE; Lebanon landing 15 Jul a MINOR reassurance. 14) 1 Jan 1959 Castro; Bay of Pigs 17-19 Apr 1961 — US loss MAJOR ('who lost Cuba'); note Kennedy's approval rose to 83% after the failure (Gallup, May 1961): publics rally on visible losses before they punish. 15) 24 Jul 1959 Kitchen Debate, Sokolniki Park — the consumer-standard dimension made explicit ('you may be ahead in rocket thrust, we are ahead in colour television'); MODERATE both ways; Khrushchev's May 1957 pledge to overtake the US in meat, milk and butter per capita is the Soviet framing. 16) 1960 'Year of Africa': 17 new UN members (Sept-Oct 1960), Res. 1514 on colonial independence (14 Dec 1960, 89-0-9, US abstaining), Khrushchev's troika campaign — the Western 'automatic majority' ends; from 1961 the US must use the 'important question' device on the China seat (Res. 1668, 15 Dec 1961, 61-34-7); the Albanian resolution ties 47-47 in Nov 1965; Soviet elite claim MAJOR. 17) 1 May 1960 U-2 shoot-down, Paris summit collapse 16-17 May 1960; Aug 1960 USIA five-country prestige survey finding pluralities in Britain and France expecting Soviet leadership within a decade, suppressed by the administration and leaked in the last week of Oct 1960 — the poll itself became the campaign's scoreboard; Kennedy's 'prestige' theme; public MODERATE, elite MAJOR. 18) 12 Apr 1961 Gagarin — Soviet SEISMIC; the Webb-McNamara memorandum (8 May 1961) tells Kennedy that 'dramatic achievements in space are being increasingly identified as a major indicator of world leadership'; the 25 May 1961 moon pledge formalises space as a score dimension. 19) 4 Jun 1961 Vienna — Khrushchev believes he has bullied Kennedy (Kennedy to Reston: 'he beat the hell out of me'); 13 Aug 1961 the Wall — the East concedes the refugee vote (about 2.7 million had left since 1949); Kennedy privately: 'a wall is a hell of a lot better than a war'; Western public reads inaction as loss MODERATE; reclaimed as a Western prestige point at 'Ich bin ein Berliner' (26 Jun 1963). 20) 17-31 Oct 1961 22nd Congress adopts the Third Party Programme: surpass US per-capita output by 1970, 'the material and technical basis of communism' by 1980; Tsar Bomba (30 Oct 1961) during the Congress; Western elite took the growth race seriously (JEC hearings 'Comparisons of the US and Soviet Economies', 1959; Samuelson's 1961 textbook chart projecting Soviet overtaking between 1984 and 1997; CIA put Soviet GNP near 45-50% of US, later shown to be overstated). 21) 16-28 Oct 1962 Cuba — both claim: Rusk's 'the other fellow just blinked' (24 Oct); Khrushchev's 12 Dec 1962 Supreme Soviet speech books a saved Cuba and a no-invasion pledge; Beijing calls it 'adventurism then capitulationism'; the shared point was catastrophe avoided, cashed jointly as the hotline (20 Jun 1963) and the Limited Test Ban Treaty (5 Aug 1963), which world opinion scored as a win for both; the Presidium's private verdict was a loss and figures in the 14 Oct 1964 ouster. 22) 1962-64 the meat-milk-butter race collapses: Novocherkassk price riots (2 Jun 1962), the 1963 harvest failure and grain purchases from Canada and the US; the earlier Riazan 'meat miracle' fraud (Larionov's suicide, Sept 1960) is the canonical case of a planner scoring himself on REPORTED figures. 23) 1965-66 Third World reversals: Ben Bella deposed (19 Jun 1965), the Indonesian PKI destroyed after 30 Sep 1965, Nkrumah overthrown (24 Feb 1966) — Soviet/Chinese losses MAJOR in Moscow's own count of 'states of national democracy', near-invisible to Western publics; simultaneously the Sino-Soviet split (advisers withdrawn Jul 1960, public from 1963, Ussuri clashes Mar 1969) is the largest single shift in the correlation of forces of the whole window. 24) Vietnam and the moon: McNaughton's 70/20/10 memo (24 Mar 1965) makes credibility the explicit score term; Tet (30 Jan 1968) and Cronkite (27 Feb 1968) collapse it domestically, SEISMIC public; Czechoslovakia (20-21 Aug 1968) costs Moscow its Western communist parties and yields the Brezhnev Doctrine (Nov 1968); Apollo 11 (20 Jul 1969) closes the space score SEISMIC for the US while the N1 fails (21 Feb and 3 Jul 1969) and Moscow denies there was ever a race.
findings.evidence: Gallup presidential approval series; Chalmers Roberts, Washington Post, 20 Dec 1957; Osgood 'Total Cold War' (2006) on USIA polling; Robert Divine 'The Sputnik Challenge' (1993); Logsdon 'John F. Kennedy and the Race to the Moon' (2010) reproducing the 8 May 1961 Webb-McNamara memo; Fursenko & Naftali 'Khrushchev's Cold War' (2006) on Vienna, Berlin and the Presidium's Cuba verdict; Westad 'The Global Cold War' (2005) chs. 4-6 on the Third World count; Taubman 'Khrushchev' (2003) on the 1957 pledge, Riazan and Novocherkassk; UN Yearbook 1960, 1961, 1965 for roll-calls; Pentagon Papers (Gravel ed.) vol. III for the McNaughton memo.

findings.title: The Soviet system kept score on rates and headcounts; the American on levels and allies. A scoreboard that scores levels only makes the USSR unwinnable; one that scores rates only makes it unbeatable
findings.detail: US GNP was roughly three times Soviet GNP in 1950 and still more than double in 1970 by any later reconstruction; the Soviet claim to be winning rested entirely on growth rates (CIA estimated 6-7% a year in the 1950s against 3% for the US, and the Soviets reported more) and on counting new states. The 1961 Programme is a pure rate-extrapolation. Contemporaries were therefore able to disagree honestly: Washington scored the level and its alliances; Moscow scored the derivative and the map. For a single scoring system usable by both superpowers, the era score must carry both a MOMENTUM term (change since the last checkpoint, which the planner can lead early) and a STANDING term (level at the checkpoint, which the market leads throughout). Historically momentum flipped around 1963-65 (harvest failure, Kosygin's Sept 1965 reforms as an admission of slowdown, CIA 'Soviet growth is slowing' estimates from 1963), so a hands-off run should show the USSR ahead on momentum at 1955 and 1960 and behind on both by 1970 — that is the calibration target.
findings.evidence: CIA/ORR estimates in the Joint Economic Committee compendia 'Comparisons of the United States and Soviet Economies' (1959) and 'Dimensions of Soviet Economic Power' (1962); Rowen & Wolf, 'The Impoverished Superpower' (1990) on the overstatement; Samuelson, 'Economics' 5th ed. (1961) fig. on Soviet-US GNP; the Third Party Programme (31 Oct 1961); Hanson, 'The Rise and Fall of the Soviet Economy' (2003) ch. 3-4.

findings.title: Losses are scored publicly and asymmetrically; covert wins are not scored at all. 'Who lost X' is the mechanism that turned alignment into domestic politics
findings.detail: The single most reliable pattern in the record: a country visibly leaving your column costs you far more at home than gaining one earns, and a covert gain earns nothing publicly. China 1949 produced McCarthyism; Cuba 1959-61 dominated the 1960 campaign; the 'loss of Laos' drove Kennedy's Southeast Asia policy in 1961; Iran 1953 and Guatemala 1954, both real gains, were unmentionable because deniable. The Soviet side had the same asymmetry in a different currency: Hungary 1956 and Czechoslovakia 1968 were losses paid in legitimacy abroad, while Ghana, Indonesia and Algeria in 1965-66 were losses paid inside the Politburo's own 'states of national democracy' ledger. The implication for design: the loss of a battleground should print a headline in your own paper ('WHO LOST CUBA?') and debit a domestic term weighted roughly three times a gain of equal size, while a gain by a deniable operation debits nothing and credits nothing publicly until it is exposed (at which point it is scored as a legitimacy loss, per the existing ladder). Credibility follows from the same rule: what allies believe about your willingness to accept a visible loss is the McNaughton 70%.
findings.evidence: Acheson, 'Present at the Creation' (1969) on the China White Paper; Kennedy-Nixon fourth debate transcript (21 Oct 1960) on Cuba; Kennedy's Laos press conference (23 Mar 1961); McNaughton memo 24 Mar 1965; Fursenko & Naftali (2006) ch. 22 on the Presidium verdict on Cuba; Westad (2005) ch. 5 on Moscow's reading of 1965-66; Kahneman-style loss aversion is not needed as a citation — the asymmetry is directly observable in the 1950 and 1960 election campaigns.

findings.title: Yes, both sides plausibly believed they were winning in 1957-62, because they were reading different metrics through their own estimates. The scoreboard must therefore be two beliefs and one reckoning
findings.detail: Moscow's belief was sincere and documented: Sputnik and Gagarin, reported growth above 8%, the 1960 admission of 17 African states, Cuba turning socialist, and Khrushchev's 6 Jan 1961 speech on wars of national liberation (which Kennedy read aloud to his staff) all fed the 1961 Programme. Washington's public belief that it was losing was equally sincere (Gaither, the missile gap, the 1960 USIA polls, Kennedy's 'get this country moving again'), while its private belief, from U-2 and Corona imagery, was that it was comfortably ahead in the strategic balance. Both were right about the metrics they chose. The gap closed on the public record only with Gilpatric (Oct 1961) and on the economic record only after 1963. Design implication: during the campaign the player should see the score AS THEIR OWN INTELLIGENCE BELIEVES IT — own figures REPORTED, rival figures as estimate brackets whose width is set by intel coverage, exactly the existing paper epistemics — and the frozen checkpoint should print the reckoned truth beside the belief, so the player can discover that they were fighting a missile gap that did not exist, or that Riazan's plan fulfilment was fiction. The rival's own scorecard ('MOSCOW BELIEVES IT IS WINNING') is a natural intelligence product for pillar 3. A deliberate deception (the Tushino flyby of Jul 1955, Khrushchev's 'sausages' boast of Nov 1959) is then a verb that edits the rival's believed score, which is what those acts were for.
findings.evidence: Khrushchev speech 6 Jan 1961 (published Kommunist, Jan 1961); NIE 11-8-59 and NIE 11-8/1-61 (declassified, CIA FOIA reading room) showing the downward revision of Soviet ICBM estimates; Gilpatric speech, Hot Springs, 21 Oct 1961; Peter Roman, 'Eisenhower and the Missile Gap' (1995); Fursenko & Naftali (2006) chs. 12-16 on Khrushchev's sincerity; Osgood (2006) and the New York Times, 26-28 Oct 1960 on the leaked USIA prestige surveys; Taubman (2003) on the 1959 Riazan affair.

findings.title: The UN General Assembly was the era's one public, numeric, annual scoreboard — and the score changed because the electorate grew, not because votes flipped
findings.detail: From 1950 (Uniting for Peace, 3 Nov 1950, 52-5-2; the PRC-as-aggressor resolution, 1 Feb 1951, 44-7-9) the US could count on an 'automatic majority'; the Soviets complained about it by that name. Membership rose from 60 in 1950 to 76 after the 1955 package deal to 99 after 1960 and 126 by 1968; the new members were the decolonized states, and the arithmetic, not defections, ended the majority. The visible markers were the 1960 colonial declaration with the US abstaining, the switch to the 'important question' device on the China seat in 1961, and the 47-47 tie in 1965. This is why a UNGA line is worth having even though the design doc correctly notes it is tautological with alignment: it is the DISPLAY UNIT contemporaries used, it is annual (September session), it is a single integer everyone understood, and it automatically shows the player the consequence of the newborn-states mechanic already in the sim. Recommend one flagship roll-call a year derived from alignment bands plus membership, printed as 'THE ASSEMBLY: 61 FOR, 34 AGAINST, 7 ABSTAINING — THE MAJORITY HOLDS / SLIPS / IS GONE'.
findings.evidence: UN Yearbook 1950, 1951, 1955, 1960, 1961, 1965 roll-calls; Res. 1514 (XV) 14 Dec 1960; Res. 1668 (XVI) 15 Dec 1961; Res. 2758 (XXVI) 25 Oct 1971 for the endpoint outside the window; Luard, 'A History of the United Nations' vol. 2 (1989); Khrushchev at the 15th session (Sept-Oct 1960) and the troika proposal.

findings.title: Prestige dimensions switched on at datable moments: the scoreboard itself has a history
findings.detail: Nobody scored space before 4 Oct 1957; nobody scored Olympic points tables before the Soviet debut at Helsinki (Jul 1952), where both press systems printed an unofficial 'team points' table and Moscow briefly claimed a 494-494 tie; nobody polled foreign prestige systematically before USIA's research office (1954); growth-rate comparisons became a public sport only after Khrushchev's 'we will bury you' (18 Nov 1956) and the 1957 meat-and-milk pledge; the consumer standard became a score term at Sokolniki in 1959. Each side then chose the count that flattered it: at Tokyo 1964 the US press counted golds (36 to 30) and the Soviet press counted medals (96 to 90), and both printed a win. Design implication: score terms should be unlocked by dated events (an 'era scoreboard' that grows from four lines in 1950 to six by 1961), and the newspaper's choice of which count to headline is itself bloc-flavoured. A sudden new dimension arriving with a rival first (Sputnik) is the historically correct way to deliver a shock without a raw number.
findings.evidence: Helsinki 1952 official report and Pravda/AP unofficial tables discussed in Riordan, 'Sport in Soviet Society' (1977); Tokyo 1964 medal counts (IOC); USIA Office of Research founding 1954 (Osgood 2006); Khrushchev at the Polish embassy 18 Nov 1956 (NYT 19 Nov 1956); Divine 'The Sputnik Challenge' (1993); the 1958 Brussels Expo and the 1959 exhibition exchange (Hixson, 'Parting the Curtain', 1997).

findings.title: Middle and minor powers were scored by contemporaries on the same dimensions read relative to their own position, and the militarily defeated side could take the point
findings.detail: Nasser lost the 1956 war and won the era: Suez made him the leader of Arab nationalism, and the Baghdad Pact never recovered; Nehru's prestige rested on hosting the non-aligned field (Bandung 1955, Belgrade 1961) and collapsed with the 1962 border war with China; Tito's score was survival as an independent communist state plus Belgrade 1961; de Gaulle's was the 1960 bomb and the 1966 NATO exit as sovereignty points; Britain's was the 1952 bomb and the 1957 Defence White Paper's admission that it could no longer afford the full ledger. In every case the contemporaries' terms were the same six, but read as change from the country's own 1950 baseline (sovereignty kept, standing inside or outside the blocs, living standard, catastrophe avoided) rather than as a share of the world. That is the warrant for one scoring function for all 86 nations: score each term as delta versus own 1950 baseline and versus the checkpoint's regional field, so that a minor's 'I stayed out of both columns and doubled my living standard' and a superpower's 'I hold Europe and lost Asia' come out of the same arithmetic with different headline lines.
findings.evidence: Kyle, 'Suez' (1991) on Nasser's post-1956 standing; Guha, 'India after Gandhi' (2007) ch. 15 on 1962; Rajak, 'Yugoslavia and the Soviet Union in the Early Cold War' (2011); the 1957 Sandys Defence White Paper (Cmnd. 124); Westad (2005) on the non-aligned auction.

findings.title: Nuclear war was never scored as winnable by the people keeping score; the era's own language supplies the pyrrhic verdict
findings.detail: NSC-68 itself, the Gaither Report and the 1957 Rockefeller Brothers report all describe general war as a catastrophe to be deterred, not a contest to be won; Eisenhower's reaction to the first SIOP briefing (Nov 1960) and Kennedy's 22 Oct 1962 line that 'even the fruits of victory would be ashes in our mouth' are the elite verdict, and Khrushchev's 1956 abandonment of the inevitability-of-war doctrine is the Soviet one. Contemporaries counted crisis DE-ESCALATION as a joint win: the 1955 Austrian State Treaty, the 1963 hotline and test ban, the 1968 NPT were scored as prestige for both signatories. So the 'avoided catastrophe' term should be a positive line that both sides earn together (treaties, crises resolved short of the top rungs), and a general exchange should not zero the score but multiply every other term by what survives, so the funeral screen can print 'you finished ahead on a board no one is left to read' — the pyrrhic verdict the vision asks for, in the period's own words.
findings.evidence: NSC-68 section VII; Gaither Report (1957) conclusions; Rockefeller Brothers Fund, 'International Security: The Military Aspect' (Jan 1958); Kennedy address 22 Oct 1962; Khrushchev's 20th Congress report (14 Feb 1956) on war not being 'fatalistically inevitable'; Burr & Rosenberg on the Nov 1960 SIOP-62 briefing (International Security 7:4, 1983, and NSA EBB 130).

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: One era scorecard with six lines, each printed as a band word plus a MOMENTUM arrow and a STANDING word, computed monthly and frozen at the checkpoints
mechanics_recommendations.why: Contemporaries tracked exactly these six (strategic balance, economic momentum/standard, the alignment ledger, prestige, bloc cohesion, credibility), and the USSR led on momentum in 1955-60 while the US led on standing throughout; scoring only level makes Moscow unplayable, scoring only rate makes it unbeatable. Both terms are cheap derivations of state the sim already has (arsenal counts, industry and living-standard series, influence standings, legitimacy, crisis outcomes).
mechanics_recommendations.how: STANDING = the checkpoint value versus the regional field; MOMENTUM = change since the last checkpoint (1950 for the first). The paper's THE WORLD IN NUMBERS gets one line: a verdict sentence such as 'AHEAD ON POINTS, LOSING GROUND IN ASIA'. At 1955/1960/1965 THE RECKONING prints the six lines with both words. The final verdict at 1970 (or on catastrophe) is the six standings plus the count of eras in which you led momentum. The per-line decision it changes: strategic balance sets the alert and arms-race verbs; momentum sets guns-vs-butter; ledger sets slot placement; prestige sets project choice; cohesion sets crush/tolerate; credibility sets crisis back-down.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Believed score versus reckoned score: the running scorecard is your own intelligence's estimate; the checkpoint freezes the truth and prints the gap
mechanics_recommendations.why: 1957-62 is the era in which both sides sincerely believed they were winning because each read its own reported figures and its own estimates of the rival (the missile gap, CIA's overstated Soviet GNP, Riazan's fictitious meat). A single objective running score would erase the best-documented dynamic of the period and the house rule that planners see REPORTED figures.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Own terms use the existing REPORTED-vs-actual economy columns; rival terms use the existing intel-bracket helpers, so the strategic-balance line reads 'MISSILES: BEHIND (EST. 3:1 AGAINST)' when coverage is thin. At the freeze the paper prints belief beside truth ('YOU BELIEVED 3:1 AGAINST; IT WAS 6:1 FOR'). The rival's own scorecard is a stealable intelligence product ('MOSCOW BELIEVES IT IS WINNING'), and a deception verb (a flyby, a boast) edits the rival's believed line, which is the Tushino 1955 mechanic. Decision changed: whether to spend on intelligence coverage before spending on the arms race.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Loss attribution: a battleground leaving your column in public prints WHO LOST X? and debits a domestic line at roughly three times the credit of a gain; deniable gains credit nothing until exposed
mechanics_recommendations.why: China 1949, Cuba 1959-61 and Laos 1961 drove US politics far more than Iran 1953 and Guatemala 1954 helped it; Moscow's 1965-66 losses in Ghana, Indonesia and Algeria hit its own ledger the same way. Loss asymmetry is what made alignment a domestic issue and what created the credibility trap of Vietnam.
mechanics_recommendations.how: On a band crossing against the player in a battleground the paper leads with the headline and the credibility line falls one band; a covert flip on the CLEAN rung credits the ledger term only (no prestige), while the EXPOSED rung debits legitimacy as it already does. Cap the credibility debit per era so escalating to avoid a loss can cost more than the loss (the 70/20/10 lesson). Decision changed: whether to commit to hold a wobbling client or accept the headline.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Dated score dimensions and dated prestige firsts: terms switch on by event (space 1957, growth race 1956-57, consumer standard 1959), and firsts are winner-take-all races on existing project machinery
mechanics_recommendations.why: Nobody scored space before Sputnik or living standards before Sokolniki; the arrival of a new dimension with a rival's first is how the real shocks landed (Sputnik moved Eisenhower's approval by twenty points without any number being printed). A second-place first earned nothing (Shepard after Gagarin; the N1 after Apollo).
mechanics_recommendations.how: Milestones (first satellite, first man in orbit, first lunar landing, first thermonuclear test) are projects whose completion by anyone credits the prestige line to the first finisher only and unlocks the dimension for everyone; the paper prints the headline and, for the loser, a 'GAP' story. Keep the count small (six to eight firsts across twenty years) so the prestige line is a handful of dated events, not a bar. Decision changed: which long project to fund and when to concede a race.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: An annual Assembly roll-call as the ledger's public integer
mechanics_recommendations.why: The UNGA count was the one public numeric scoreboard of the era, and it changed because the electorate grew (60 members in 1950, 99 by 1960) rather than because votes flipped — which is exactly what the sim's newborn-states mechanic produces. The design doc calls this tautological with alignment; it is, but it is the display unit contemporaries used and it makes the decolonization wave legible as a single number.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Each September, one flagship roll-call: FOR/AGAINST/ABSTAIN derived from alignment bands of member states (non-aligned abstain), printed with a verdict ('THE MAJORITY HOLDS / SLIPS / IS GONE') and, from 1961, the 'important question' story when the two-thirds device becomes necessary. No new state, no votes to buy in v1. Decision changed: whether to court newborn states before their first session.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Avoided catastrophe as a shared positive line, and a general exchange as a survival multiplier rather than a zero
mechanics_recommendations.why: Contemporaries scored de-escalation as a joint prestige win (Austria 1955, the hotline and test ban 1963, the NPT 1968) and never scored general war as winnable; Kennedy's 'ashes in our mouth' and Khrushchev's 1956 doctrine are the period's own verdict. The vision wants Armageddon shared and 'winning' one pyrrhic.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Treaties and crises resolved below the top rungs credit both parties' avoided-catastrophe line and legitimacy (already the world-opinion currency). A general exchange ends the campaign through the existing GameOver funeral, which prints the six lines multiplied by the surviving population fraction and the sentence 'ahead on a board no one is left to read'. Decision changed: whether to take the compromise branch of a crisis when the ledger says you would win the standoff.

pitfalls: Scoring the superpowers on absolute economic level alone: US GNP was roughly three times Soviet GNP in 1950 and still more than double in 1970, so a level-only board tells the Soviet player they are losing from the first paper; contemporaries scored momentum, which is why Moscow could believe it was winning until 1963.

Scoring only the objective truth during the campaign: it erases the missile gap, the overstated Soviet GNP, the Riazan fraud and the whole 1957-62 double belief, and it breaks the house rule that planners read REPORTED figures and foreign numbers are estimates. Conversely, scoring only belief makes the game unfalsifiable; the checkpoint reconciliation is the fix.

Counting the Third World by headcount: Guinea (1958) and Ghana (1957) then outweigh Egypt or India; both Moscow's own 'states of national democracy' list and CIA's aid tables weighted by population and position. Use the existing battleground weights.

Switching on prestige, space or Olympic terms in 1950: nobody kept score on space before Sputnik or living standards before 1959, and a 1950 board with six lines is noise; terms must arrive with dated events, and a rival first must be able to arrive as a shock rather than a bar filling.

Making prestige or credibility a spendable resource (EU4/Vic-style): every contemporary measure was a verdict derived from events (polls, votes, firsts, crises), never a bank; the influence research already killed fungible influence for snowballing, and prestige-as-currency snowballs the same way.

Uncapped loss aversion: if 'who lost X' debits are unbounded the player escalates every wobbling client into Vietnam because the loss always costs more than the war; McNaughton's 70% is the historical warning. Cap the credibility debit per era so escalation can cost more than the headline.

A second scoring function for minors: the same six terms read as delta from own 1950 baseline handle Nasser (lost the war, won the era), Tito, Nehru and Ghana without special cases; a bespoke minor-power victory is how QMG-style third factions ended up needing their own win condition.

Letting a nuclear exchange yield a winner: no period document scored general war as winnable, and the vision forbids it; a survival multiplier on the funeral screen keeps the campaign playable to the end while keeping the verdict pyrrhic.
analysts.first_hour_test: In the founding edition (January 1950) the player should read one verdict sentence in THE WORLD IN NUMBERS and nothing else about score: for the USA, 'AHEAD ON EVERY COUNT, SHAKEN IN ASIA' (China lost in October 1949, the Soviet bomb announced 23 September 1949, the H-bomb decision of 31 January 1950 as the first lead story); for the USSR, 'BEHIND IN STRENGTH, GAINING GROUND' (the bomb, China, the reported growth rate); for a minor, 'OUTSIDE THE BLOCS, STANDING STILL' or 'IN WASHINGTON'S COLUMN, STANDING STILL'. The scoreboard at this date has four lines, not six: strategic balance (rival figures as estimate brackets), economic momentum (own REPORTED, rival estimated), the alignment ledger (the existing regional standings), and cohesion; prestige and credibility switch on with their first events. In April 1950 an NSC-68-style event (or its Soviet mirror) hands the player the framing and one decision: accept the zero-sum reading (the ledger line gains its 'who lost X' debit and the military budget verbs unlock) or reject it. By June 1950 the player should have seen exactly one line move — the ledger, if Korea's approach has shifted a battleground — and no term should have moved more than one band. At the first checkpoint (1 January 1955) THE RECKONING front page prints the six-line board with MOMENTUM and STANDING words and, beside each rival line, what the player believed against what was true; a hands-off US run should read 'AHEAD ON POINTS, BEHIND ON MOMENTUM: Korea drawn, Indochina slipping, Tehran and Guatemala City quietly held, Moscow claims the hydrogen bomb', and a hands-off Soviet run the mirror, 'GAINING ON EVERY FRONT BUT STRENGTH'. If either superpower reads the 1955 board as a clear win or a clear loss, the weights are wrong.

findings.title: Twilight Struggle already gives you the region formula; what it does NOT give you is a balanced opening board, and UGS's battleground set is structurally Western
findings.detail: Twilight Struggle (GMT Games, 2005; Deluxe Ed. 2009, rules 10.1) scores each region when its card is played: Presence / Domination / Control are worth Europe 3/7/auto-win, Asia 3/7/9, Middle East 3/5/7, Africa 1/4/6, Central America 1/3/5, South America 2/5/6, plus +1 VP per battleground controlled and +1 per country adjacent to the enemy superpower. UGS's `verdict()` in crates/ugs-sim/src/influence.rs already implements the TS shape (Control = threshold AND rival 0; Domination = threshold AND mine > rival; Presence = 1) over 41 sourced battlegrounds. But TS's marker starts at 0 with a deliberately balanced starting placement; UGS's 1950 board is not balanced because every Soviet holding (Poland, GDR, PRC, the satellites) is LOCKED and therefore not a battleground, while the contestable set is mostly Western-held or neutral. Applying the TS values to the hands-off harness output (`cargo test -p ugs-sim hands_off_bands -- --ignored --nocapture`, run today): 1955 board = EUROPE W Dom 7+6 = 13, ASIA W Pres 3+3 = 6, CENTRAL_AMERICA W Control 5+3 = 8, MIDDLE_EAST W Pres 3+2 = 5, SOUTH_AMERICA W Dom 5+4 = 9, AFRICA 0 -> West 41, East 0. 1960: West 35 (East gets Presence in ME and Africa). 1965: West 28 (East Presence in Asia, ME, Africa, Central America after Cuba). Scored absolutely, the West leads +28 in 1965 — past TS's 20-VP auto-win, a blowout. Scored as DELTA from the 1950 par (the TS way: the marker starts at zero on the opening placement), the same run reads 0 / -6 / -7 per era, i.e. East +13 by 1965: 'the East is gaining in the Third World' falls straight out of the existing sim with no new tuning. Tournament TS handles side imbalance the same way — by bidding starting influence for the USSR, never by changing the scoring table — which is the precedent for 'fix the par, not the formula'.
findings.evidence: Twilight Struggle Deluxe rules 10.1.1-10.1.3 (scoring), 10.2 (final scoring; VP 0 = draw); WBC/online tournament side-bidding convention (twilightstrategy.com 'Bidding'); Playdek/Wargameroom win-rate data 2012-13 showing ~55-60% USSR wins, addressed by bids not rules. UGS: influence.rs `compute_standings`/`verdict`, influence.ron thresholds (EUROPE 1/5/8, MIDDLE_EAST 1/4/6, ASIA 1/5/8, AFRICA 1/4/7, CENTRAL_AMERICA 1/2/3, SOUTH_AMERICA 1/3/5); hands-off table in the scratchpad run (1955 W41/E0, 1960 W35/E0+, 1965 W28 with East Presence in four regions).

findings.title: Periodic scoring beats end-only scoring for three mechanical reasons, and snapshot-deltas beat integrals for a fourth that is specific to UGS
findings.detail: (1) Feedback inside the campaign: a player must learn the price of a coup or an aid slot before the 20-year verdict; TS's scoring cards, Pax Pamir's Dominance Checks and Terraforming Mars' milestones all put a reckoning within the player's planning horizon. (2) Banking: what is scored at a checkpoint cannot be undone — TS's Europe scoring in turn 3 stays scored even if Europe flips by turn 9; UGS's frozen 1955 standings already do this, and it is the mechanism that makes a 1958 Iraq revolution or a 1959 Cuba a story rather than an erasure. (3) Rhythm: a known cadence gives the real-time game a turn structure it otherwise lacks (Pax Pamir shows the next Dominance Check in the market row; Terraforming Mars players count generations to the end). (4) The UGS-specific reason NOT to integrate monthly the way Through the Ages accumulates culture every turn: the 1950 board is asymmetric (+41 West under TS values), so an integral would multiply the structural lead by 240 months and drown every player decision; Through the Ages can integrate because every player starts identical. Therefore: standings are computed monthly (already), printed monthly as a PROVISIONAL line, but only four snapshots count — 1955, 1960, 1965 and the 1970 close — and each era's score is the change since the previous snapshot, so the sum of the four era reckonings equals the board relative to 1950 par (a legibility identity the paper can print).
findings.evidence: Pax Pamir 2nd ed. rulebook (Wehrlegig, 2019) Dominance Check: 4 cards in the deck, visible in the market before resolution; Terraforming Mars (FryxGames 2016) milestones (first to claim, 8 MC, 5 VP) vs awards (funded 8/14/20 MC, scored at end 5/2 VP); Through the Ages: A New Story of Civilization (CGE 2015) culture as a per-turn integral; Twilight Struggle 10.1 'scoring cards must be played the turn drawn'. UGS: `Checkpoint { year, standings, totals }` frozen at CHECKPOINT_YEARS [1955,1960,1965] in influence.rs; newspaper.md 'date-stamped, still' house rule.

findings.title: The auto-win threshold is a threat, not a tally; UGS should not copy it but must replace its function — the trailing side's desperation
findings.detail: TS's 20-VP automatic victory (rules 3.x/10.3) changes play because a marker at 15 is a threat that forces the trailing player into coups at DEFCON risk and into 'Wargames' (card #99: at DEFCON 2 the phasing player may end the game immediately by giving the opponent 6 VP — a bounded, pyrrhic cash-out of a lead). Pax Pamir has the same device (the game ends after a Dominance Check if one player leads by 4 or more VP). UGS runs to 1970 by design and its thesis is 'the century without ending the world', so an early auto-win would cut off the escalation pillar precisely when it matters. Keep the function two ways: (a) an era graded DECISIVE (lead >= 12 in superpower scale) is printed as such, and two consecutive DECISIVE eras stamp 'THE CENTURY IS DECIDED' on the paper without ending play (Civilization's score screen model: the record is fixed, the world continues); (b) the trailing pole's AI reads the ledger gap as risk appetite — the existing coup gate and crisis escalate-vs-back-down choices get a modifier from (rival era score - own era score), so a Moscow that is losing the map in 1963 runs coups at CHANCES ABOUT EVEN where a winning Moscow waits for PROBABLE. That is TS's runaway effect reproduced as pillar-1 behaviour rather than as a rule: the losing side courts DEFCON. It is deterministic (an integer read at the monthly allocator) and it is the one place the score should feed back into the sim.
findings.evidence: Twilight Struggle Deluxe rules: 20 VP automatic victory; Wargames card text ('If DEFCON level is 2, you may immediately end the game (without Final Scoring) after giving opponent 6 VP'); Military Ops requirement (a per-turn VP penalty for failing to meet DEFCON) as an example of scoring driving aggression. Pax Pamir 2e early-end rule. UGS: influence.rs AI allocator (monthly, USA/SOV, score by weight/pop/contest, no coups in v1); crisis.rs escalate/back-down through the command log; tension.md AI note (Brink = everyone seeks off-ramps).

findings.title: Shared loss needs its own track that overrides the score lexicographically — otherwise the leader computes whether Armageddon is 'worth it'
findings.detail: TS's DEFCON is orthogonal to the VP track: DEFCON 1 ends the game and the player who caused it loses regardless of VP (rules 8.x); Labyrinth (GMT 2010) ends instantly on a WMD detonating in the US regardless of the prestige/resource race; Balance of Power (Crawford, 1985) refuses to score a nuclear war at all ('We do not reward failure' — the line UGS's endgame.rs already prints). If a general exchange were merely '-50 points', a player 60 ahead would take it. So the verdict must be a pair (CATASTROPHE state, score), ordered CATASTROPHE first. Three states from existing sim facts: UNSCARRED; SCARRED = the nuclear taboo broken by your bloc (`taboo_broken`, the MacArthur chain) OR own dead in the era >= 1,000,000 (`Military.casualties` + demography cohorts) OR a second CRUSH (`crushed_count`); RUINED = `GameOver` (rung 8). Grade caps: UNSCARRED may reach THE CENTURY WON; SCARRED caps at COSTLY (the verdict sentence appends the price: 'AT A PRICE: 1.2M DEAD, THE TABOO BROKEN'); RUINED prints LOST for every nation on earth — the initiator's line reads 'LOST — AND YOU FIRED FIRST', and the ledger is printed under the funeral as an epitaph ('THE LEDGER AS OF 14 OCT 1962: WEST +9. IT DID NOT MATTER.'). This makes the big war playable (a conventional WW3 won by settlement keeps every point the map gives — ClientState clauses set the patron's edge and lock) but never win-able at the top grade, and the score you kept is exactly what makes the pyrrhic verdict sting.
findings.evidence: Twilight Struggle rules 8.x DEFCON 1 ('the phasing player loses'); Labyrinth: The War on Terror rules 2.0 (Jihadist instant win on WMD in US; US wins on 12 prestige + Good-governance resources); Chris Crawford, Balance of Power (Mindscape 1985; Microsoft Press book 1986) nuclear-war screen; Nuclear War (Flying Buffalo 1965) 'if all players die nobody wins'. UGS: crisis.rs `GameOver { initiator, against, tick, dead, cities }`; endgame.rs 'THE PEACE HELD n YEARS' and 'WE DO NOT REWARD FAILURE'; escalation.md 'Failure state... always reconstructible from the command log'; war-termination.md ClientState/Neutralization clauses write alignment.

findings.title: Middle and minor powers score with the same three-line formula by changing the column, the regions and the scale — never the arithmetic (Labyrinth's asymmetric targets on one board)
findings.detail: Labyrinth gives the US and the Jihadist different win conditions read off the same board; QMG: The Cold War's third faction needed a bespoke victory and the influence research already rejected a third AI. The cheap UGS equivalent: every nation's MAP term is 'the column of the band I am in, over my regions, minus my 1950 par'. The standings already carry three columns (west, east, denied); `verdict(mine, rival, t)` works unchanged for the denied column with rival = max(west, east), so India, Egypt and Yugoslavia are scored on whether the FIELD holds their region (hands-off 1965 MIDDLE_EAST: W2 E1 N4 -> the denied column reaches Domination; Egypt's par from 1955 was N5 -> Domination too, so hands-off Egypt reads STALEMATE, which is right). A scorecard needs only three data fields per playable nation: `regions` (USA/SOV: all six; GBR: EUROPE, MIDDLE_EAST, ASIA, AFRICA; FRA: EUROPE, AFRICA, MIDDLE_EAST; IND: ASIA; ISL: EUROPE), `scale` (superpower 1, middle 2, minor 3 — the grade bands are multiplied by it, so a minor is DECISIVE at +4 where a superpower needs +12), and nothing else: the column comes from the live band, so a France that leaves NATO still scores West, and a PRC that leaves the Sino-Soviet lock (hands-off PRC is N by 1965) starts scoring the field. OUTPUT and STANDING are per-country already (industry per capita, legitimacy), so they need no scorecard at all. A minor with zero program slots still gets a verdict — Japan's century is won on OUTPUT with the map term flat, which is the historically correct game for Japan.
findings.evidence: Labyrinth rules 2.0 asymmetric victory; docs/research/influence.md principle 8 ('Never a third AI... QMG: Cold War needed a bespoke victory'); influence.rs `RegionStanding { west, east, denied }` and `verdict()`; influence.md edge case 'Player is a minor with 0 slots: read-only'; planning.rs `dashboard_industry_centi` (reported for Planned, actual for Market) and `observed_industry_centi`; settlement.rs `legitimacy: BTreeMap<CountryTag, i32>`.

findings.title: A visible running score is fine when it is provisional, monthly-stamped and worded as a counterfactual; the fixed checkpoint date replaces TS's hidden scoring timing and is bounded by flow rates
findings.detail: TS's tension comes from hidden timing (the opponent does not know when Africa scores), which a real-time game with public checkpoint dates cannot copy. Terraforming Mars shows every award leader all game and still plays well because the number that counts is taken once; Pax Pamir shows the next Dominance Check in the market. So: the paper's INFLUENCE STANDINGS gains a LEDGER box each month — 'IF THE RECKONING WERE TODAY: EAST +4 SINCE 1955 (ASIA, AFRICA)' — plus a countdown chip 'RECKONING IN 14 MO' in the HUD, and the frozen number is the only one that counts. The obvious worry, a Q4-1954 rush to flip battlegrounds before the freeze, is bounded by the existing arithmetic: AID tier 1 = 10/month, tier 3 = 30/month, x2 contested, x2 small state = at most 120/month, so a flip from 0 to the 300 band edge takes >= 3 months at the theoretical maximum and 30 months at the usual rate; hysteresis halves reversal rate for 12 months after a band change; one op slot with 90-day coup prep caps a sponsor at one coup per quarter; and elections fire on sourced calendar dates, not on the checkpoint. The rush therefore starts about eighteen months out, which is exactly the tempo TS produces when a player knows a scoring card is in the opponent's hand. The substitute for hidden timing is the election calendar and the 24-month contested windows — public, dated, and the actual 'scoring cards' of a decade.
findings.evidence: Terraforming Mars awards (public leader, scored once at end); Pax Pamir 2e market-visible Dominance Checks; Twilight Struggle 10.1 (scoring card must be played the turn it is held; holding one at turn end loses the game). UGS influence.md tuning: AID_FLOW 10 x tier, PRESENCE_FLOW 5, x2 contested/small state, BAND_ENTER 300, REVERSAL_MONTHS 12, COUP_PREP_DAYS 90, one op slot; newspaper.md section registry and 'ALL FIGURES AS OF {date}'.

findings.title: The economy term is where the West's structural strength belongs — as a score line, not a drift — and it is the one knob that decides where hands-off lands
findings.detail: The influence skeptics killed living-standard drift because it repainted the Third World West; the research deferred 'the systems-competition term as a checkpoint score line'. Scoring is the safe place for it because a score line moves no country. With MAP scored as deltas from 1950 par, the hands-off map term runs 0 / -6 / -7 / (est. -3 for 1965-70) = East +16 over the campaign. An OUTPUT term of clamp((own actual industry per capita - rival's) / step, -4, +4) per era, taken from `actual_centi` (never `reported_centi` — the reckoning tells the planner the truth his dashboard did not) runs about +3 to +4 West per era = +14, and a STANDING term from legitimacy bands (>= +25: +3; 0..24: +1; -24..-1: -1; <= -25: -3) runs about +4 West over four eras (UNSC 83 grants the US >= 25 in 1950; a Soviet CRUSH in 1956 debits). Net hands-off: -16 + 14 + 4 = +2 West: NARROW WESTERN, EAST GAINING IN ASIA, AFRICA AND THE MIDDLE EAST — the brief's target, from three terms. The MAP term must never be tuned to hit this (it is the pillar); the OUTPUT cap (+/-4) and the STANDING band values are the knobs, and the harness should assert the result: final hands-off in [+1, +6] West, MAP sum <= -10, East verdict >= Presence in at least three regions by 1965. Note that `LivingStandards` is static in v1, so the term must read industry per capita until SoL moves.
findings.evidence: docs/research/influence.md 'What the skeptics killed' and 'Deferred' (systems-competition term as a checkpoint score line); demography.rs `LivingStandards` ('Static in v1'); planning.rs actual vs reported centi; settlement.rs test 'UNSC 83 grants legitimacy' (>= 25); hands-off harness deltas computed above (1955 41, 1960 35, 1965 28 under TS values); Twilight Struggle's structural asymmetry handled by a fixed +/-VP bid rather than by re-weighting regions.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: THE LEDGER: one integer score per nation per era from three terms plus a par
mechanics_recommendations.why: Legible (three ledger lines, each a named integer), deterministic (reads frozen checkpoint state, integer arithmetic, BTreeMaps), cheap (226 nations x 4 eras x 5 ints, computed once at each freeze), and pole-agnostic: the formula never branches on nation; only the column, the regions and the scale differ. It turns the existing standings into a score without a second system, and the TS region values give the map term its weight (Europe and the Americas matter more than Africa) where UGS's current thresholds only give verdict words.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Per region r, per column c in {west, east, denied}: points(r, c) = value(verdict(count_c, max of other columns, thresholds_r)) + count_c, with TS values Presence/Domination/Control = EUROPE 3/7/12, ASIA 3/7/10, MIDDLE_EAST 3/5/7, AFRICA 1/4/6, CENTRAL_AMERICA 1/3/5, SOUTH_AMERICA 2/5/6 (data, in influence.ron next to thresholds). MAP(nation, era) = sum over the nation's regions of [points(r, my column) - points(r, strongest other column)] minus the same quantity frozen at 1950-01-01 (the par; a fourth 'checkpoint' at tick 0 with year 1950). OUTPUT(nation, era) = clamp((actual industry per 1,000 pop - rival's) / STEP, -4, +4), rival = the other pole's leader for a bloc member, the world median for the field. STANDING(nation, era) = band of `legitimacy_of` (>= 25: +3, 0..24: +1, -24..-1: -1, <= -25: -3). Era score = MAP + OUTPUT + STANDING; campaign score = sum of the four eras (1955, 1960, 1965, 1970). Grade bands scaled by the scorecard's `scale` (1 superpower, 2 middle, 3 minor): STALEMATE |s x scale| <= 1, NARROW 2-5, CLEAR 6-11, DECISIVE >= 12. Scorecard rows (regions, scale) live in scenario data; default for an unlisted country = its own region, scale 3. Column = the nation's live band at the freeze (Denied for NonAligned). Hands-off target asserted in the calibration harness: campaign +1..+6 West, MAP <= -10, OUTPUT >= +10.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: THE RECKONING: fixed-date era freezes with a graded verdict sentence, plus a provisional monthly line and a countdown
mechanics_recommendations.why: Periodic scoring gives feedback, banks history (Cuba flips after 1960 without erasing the 1960 record) and gives a real-time campaign a turn rhythm. Public dates replace TS's hidden timing; the flow-rate bounds (>= 3 months per flip even at maximum, 12-month hysteresis, one coup per quarter) keep the pre-checkpoint rush an eighteen-month campaign rather than a last-week exploit. A visible-but-provisional number is the Terraforming Mars pattern and satisfies 'computed verdict sentence' and 'monthly date-stamped still'.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Extend the existing checkpoint freeze (influence.rs, `new_month` && January && CHECKPOINT_YEARS) with 1970 as the close and 1950 as the par, and write an `EraReckoning { year, map, output, standing, catastrophe, casualties, grade }` per nation into the checkpoint. The paper's THE RECKONING page prints, for the player, both poles and the field: the six regional verdict words, the three ledger lines as signed integers with their cause ('MAP -6: AFRICA LOST TO PRESENCE, MIDDLE EAST CONTESTED'), the grade word, and the identity line 'SUM OF THE ERAS = THE BOARD SINCE 1950'. Every other month the INFLUENCE STANDINGS section carries a LEDGER box 'IF THE RECKONING WERE TODAY: EAST +4 SINCE 1960 (ASIA, AFRICA)' rendered from the same function against live standings, plus a HUD chip 'RECKONING IN 14 MO'. Two consecutive DECISIVE eras stamp 'THE CENTURY IS DECIDED' on the masthead; play continues. Foreign OUTPUT prints through `observed_industry_centi` with an EST. bracket in the monthly line and the truth at the freeze — the reckoning is the one page where the planner's own reported figure and the actual figure sit side by side.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: THE CATASTROPHE TRACK: a lexicographic gate above the score with three states and grade caps
mechanics_recommendations.why: Shared loss must live on a separate track (TS DEFCON, Labyrinth WMD, Balance of Power's refusal to score) or a leader will price Armageddon. Grade caps make the big war playable but never the best outcome, and they make the pyrrhic win legible: your score stands, printed, and does not matter.
mechanics_recommendations.how: State per nation per era, computed at the freeze from existing facts: UNSCARRED; SCARRED if the nation's bloc broke the taboo this era (`taboo_broken` attributable to it), or own dead in the era >= 1,000,000 (`Military.casualties` delta plus civilian cohorts killed by battlefield use), or `crushed_count` rose to >= 2; RUINED when `GameOver` exists (all nations, all eras thereafter). The campaign verdict = (worst catastrophe state, sum of era scores). Caps: UNSCARRED -> grades THE CENTURY WON / HELD / SLIPPING / LOST by score band; SCARRED -> best grade COSTLY, sentence appends the bill ('AT A PRICE: 1.2M DEAD, THE TABOO BROKEN AT THE YALU'); RUINED -> LOST for everyone, the initiator's line 'LOST — AND YOU FIRED FIRST', and the funeral screen gains one epitaph line 'THE LEDGER AS OF {date}: {pole} +{n}.
